compost.md.primary: A nutrient-rich biological mixture of decaying organic matter, vegetation, and manure used to fertilize and condition agricultural soil.
compost.md.secondary: In horticultural biotechnology and agronomy, controlled aerobic decomposition of biological waste products to generate microbial-dense humus for soil stabilization.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Confess yourself to heaven, repent what’s past, avoid what is to come; and do not spread the **compost** on the weeds, to make them ranker.

quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau
quotes.quote: The maker of this earth but patented a leaf, and rotting vegetation returned to fertile **compost** under the autumn rains.

quotes.author: James Joyce
quotes.quote: And also it was a marvel to see in that castle how by magic they make a **compost** out of fecund wheatkidneys out of Chaldee.

expostulate.md.primary: To express strong disapproval, disagreement, or earnest remonstrance with someone regarding their actions or conduct.
expostulate.md.secondary: In ethical discourse and interpersonal rhetoric, to present reasoned moral objections in an attempt to dissuade a companion from an imprudent course.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: My liege and madam, to **expostulate** what majesty should be, what duty is, why day is day, night night, and time is time, were nothing but to waste night, day and time.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Elizabeth-Jane ventured to **expostulate** with Henchard upon his severity toward the humble carter.

quotes.author: Bram Stoker
quotes.quote: I tried to **expostulate** with him, but he only shook his head mournfully and pointed to the gathering wolves outside the castle.

expostulation.md.primary: An earnest, impassioned remonstrance, objection, or protest voiced against another person's actions, policies, or beliefs.
expostulation.md.secondary: In literary rhetoric and moral philosophy, a formal discourse or exclamation articulating principled grievance and urging moral correction.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Nay, we must use **expostulation** kindly, for it is parting from us.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: And then her cooing voice, plaintive in **expostulation**, disturbed the darkness, the velvet touch of her lips passing over his brow.

quotes.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
quotes.quote: Coverdale raised a passionate **expostulation** against the cold fanaticism that subordinated human affection to visionary social experiments.

impost.md.primary: A tax, duty, or financial tribute levied by governmental authority, especially a customs tariff assessed on imported merchandise.
impost.md.secondary: In classical architectural engineering, the uppermost member of a pillar, wall, or pier upon which the foot of an arch immediately rests and springs.

quotes.author: Alexander Hamilton
quotes.quote: We will presume, for argument’s sake, that the revenue arising from the **impost** duties answers the purposes of a provision for the public debt.

quotes.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
quotes.quote: Pacing the Custom-House wharf, the merchant computed the heavy **impost** exacted upon each consignment of European cargo.

quotes.author: Thomas V. Cooper
quotes.quote: It became necessary to adapt our laws, and especially our laws of **impost**, to the new circumstances in which we found ourselves.

imposter.md.primary: A person who deceives others by adopting a fictitious identity, false title, or counterfeit credentials; an alternate spelling of impostor.
imposter.md.secondary: In social psychology and theatrical literature, an pretender who manufactures deceptive social masks to gain illicit standing, wealth, or sympathy.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: He looked upon her as a species of **imposter**; a guilty woman in the guise of an innocent one.

quotes.author: Joseph Conrad
quotes.quote: In the street—I don’t know why—a queer feeling came to me that I was an **imposter**.

quotes.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotes.quote: Sherlock Holmes unmasked the clever **imposter** whose aristocratic manners had duped half the fashionable salons of London.

impostor.md.primary: One who practices deception under an assumed character, fraudulent name, or counterfeit persona for selfish gain.
impostor.md.secondary: In forensic psychiatry and legal jurisprudence, an individual who executes elaborate systemic deception or impersonation to subvert trust.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: I am an **impostor** and a counterfeit, if I have not seen the gold with mine own eyes.

quotes.author: Charles Dickens
quotes.quote: The indignation of the master fell upon the shameless **impostor** whose pious pretenses had robbed the orphans of their bread.

quotes.author: G. K. Chesterton
quotes.quote: Father Brown gently exposed the self-styled holy man as an audacious **impostor** preying upon provincial superstitions.

imposture.md.primary: The practice of deception or fraudulent imposition under an assumed character or false appearance; an act of cheating.
imposture.md.secondary: In historical and philosophical criticism, the systematic manufacture and perpetuation of fraudulent claims or myths to manipulate human credulity.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.quote: Barbarous tribes are peculiarly liable to be duped by the cunning **imposture** of medicine-men and sorcerers.

quotes.author: Charles Dickens
quotes.quote: The entire family connection united in denouncing the scandalous **imposture** that had alienated the grandfather's bequest.

quotes.author: Mrs. Oliphant
quotes.quote: She recoiled from the thought of an organized **imposture**, preferring outright penury to deceitful prosperity.

post.md.primary: A sturdy upright timber, metal column, or stone pillar fixed firmly in the ground to support fences, signs, or structural beams.
post.md.secondary: An assigned military or administrative station; or the governmental apparatus and network dedicated to conveying public dispatches and letters.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Thou shalt be pinch'd as thick as honeycomb, each pinch more stinging than bees that made 'em, bound fast to this rocky **post**.

quotes.author: John Locke
quotes.quote: A sentinel assigned to an exposed **post** must remain vigilant through the darkest hours of night.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Oak leaned his broad back against the gate **post**, listening to the rhythmic murmurs of the folded sheep.

postage.md.primary: The statutory charge, fee, or rate levied by a postal service for the transport and delivery of letters, cards, and parcels.
postage.md.secondary: In fiscal history and philately, the prepaid government adhesive stamp or printed franking impression signifying payment of transmission tariffs.

quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau
quotes.quote: For my part, I could easily do without the post-office; I think that there are very few important communications made through it, and rarely worth the **postage**.

quotes.author: Elihu W. Baldwin
quotes.work: The Life and Letters of Elihu W. Baldwin
quotes.quote: He paid the heavy international **postage** on the packet of letters arriving from missionaries across the sea.

quotes.author: John Cairns
quotes.quote: Before the introduction of the penny stamp, the high cost of **postage** imposed a serious burden upon scholarly correspondence.

postal.md.primary: Relating to, belonging to, or conducted by the national public mail distribution system and its administration.
postal.md.secondary: In international communications law, denoting treaties, routes, conventions, and regulations that govern cross-border mail transit.

quotes.author: H. G. Wells
quotes.quote: He hurried past the red pillar-box and into the country **postal** office to dispatch his telegram.

quotes.author: Frank A. Fetter
quotes.quote: The state administration of the **postal** monopoly exemplifies public operation of a vital infrastructural utility.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Letters were carried by the royal **postal** couriers with a deliberate regularity that suited the slower rhythms of provincial life.

postcard.md.primary: A rectangular card of stiff paper or cardstock intended for writing and mailing a short message without an envelope.
postcard.md.secondary: In philately, tourism culture, and visual history, an illustrated photographic or lithographic mailing card produced for souvenir trade and rapid correspondence.

quotes.author: G. K. Chesterton
quotes.quote: He scribbled a brief, cryptic instruction upon the back of a picture **postcard** before dropping it into the pillar-box.

quotes.author: Grace S. Richmond
quotes.quote: She received a hastily penned **postcard** from the seaside town, bearing news of the convalescent child's recovery.

quotes.author: Meyer Moldeven
quotes.quote: He kept the faded **postcard** framed above his study desk as a memento of his first transatlantic journey.

postcava.md.primary: The inferior vena cava; the primary venous trunk that collects deoxygenated blood from the lower extremities and abdominal viscera.
postcava.md.secondary: In comparative vertebrate anatomy and cardiac physiology, the caudal or posterior great systemic vein opening directly into the right atrium of the heart.

quotes.author: Thomas Henry Huxley
quotes.work: Manual of the Anatomy of Vertebrated Animals
quotes.quote: The venous blood returning from the trunk and kidneys is collected into the great **postcava** before entering the sinus venosus.

quotes.author: Henry Gray
quotes.quote: In quadrupeds, the inferior vena cava is frequently denominated the **postcava** in accordance with anatomical orientation.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.work: The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals
quotes.quote: Comparative dissections of mammalian embryos reveal how the embryonic cardinal veins transform into the definitive **postcava**.

postcode.md.primary: An alphanumeric sequence appended to a postal address to facilitate automated sorting and rapid routing of mail.
postcode.md.secondary: In spatial geography, demographic analysis, and urban logistics, a localized geographic territory code used for census sampling and municipal delivery zoning.

quotes.author: George Orwell
quotes.quote: The municipal authorities reorganized metropolitan delivery districts, requiring every letter to display its proper **postcode**.

quotes.author: J. B. Priestley
quotes.quote: He noted how commercial districts were neatly cataloged by the new regional **postcode** system introduced by postal planners.

quotes.author: Anthony Burgess
quotes.quote: Enderby glanced at the return address on the brown envelope, noting the unfamiliar provincial **postcode** stamped upon the corner.

posted.md.primary: Displayed publicly by affixing a notice to a wall or placard; or dispatched through the postal service.
posted.md.secondary: Assigned to a specific military station, ship, or diplomatic garrison; or thoroughly informed and up-to-date regarding facts.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: O, most wicked speed, to post with such dexterity to incestuous sheets! She **posted** off to wedlock ere her tears were dry.

quotes.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotes.quote: A reward of one thousand pounds was **posted** upon every church door and police station throughout the county.

quotes.author: Herman Melville
quotes.quote: The solitary lookout was **posted** at the masthead, peering into the sunlit foam of the Pacific.

poster.md.primary: A large printed bill, decorative placard, or pictorial advertisement displayed in public places to announce events or products.
poster.md.secondary: Historically, a courier or traveler who rode with haste on post horses; or a billsticker employed to paste placards upon hoardings.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Jude caught sight of an illuminated **poster** announcing a lecture upon theological antiquities in the market town.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Crowds clustered before the tavern wall where a vibrant election **poster** proclaimed the reform candidate's manifesto.

quotes.author: Charles Dickens
quotes.quote: A billsticker with a paste-pot was diligently smoothing out an enormous theatre **poster** across the wooden fence.

posterboard.md.primary: A heavy, stiff paperboard or cardboard suitable for displaying printed signs, school projects, presentations, and artistic placards.
posterboard.md.secondary: In display design and educational visual arts, layered cellulosic card stock formulated for structural rigidity, ink receptivity, and mounting media.

quotes.author: Meyer Moldeven
quotes.quote: The students lettered their astronomical charts across sheets of heavy white **posterboard** for the science exhibition.

quotes.author: Annie Roe Carr
quotes.quote: Nan sketched colorful banners on stiff **posterboard** to decorate the assembly hall before the winter carnival.

quotes.author: Grace S. Richmond
quotes.quote: He tacked a hand-drawn notices on sturdy **posterboard** to the parish bulletin board outside the chapel gate.

posterior.md.primary: Situated at the back or toward the rear of a structure or body; or coming later in temporal sequence.
posterior.md.secondary: In anatomy and zoology, denoting dorsal or caudal positions opposite to anterior; colloquially, the human buttocks.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: The **posterior** of the day, most generous sir, is liable, congruent and measurable for the afternoon.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.quote: The **posterior** extremities in all quadrupeds exhibit homologous skeletal elements that reflect a common ancestral archetype.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: The historical sequence of events demonstrated that the legal claim was **posterior** to the original settlement.

posteriority.md.primary: The state, condition, or fact of being later in time or subsequent in sequence relative to something else.
posteriority.md.secondary: In metaphysics, chronology, and logic, the temporal or conceptual status of following an antecedent event, opposed to priority.

quotes.author: Francis Bacon
quotes.quote: The order of nature assigneth a necessary **posteriority** to secondary causes when viewed alongside the first cause.

quotes.author: Samuel Johnson
quotes.quote: The apparent **posteriority** of his verse composition to his historical prose was clearly established by surviving manuscripts.

quotes.author: John Locke
quotes.quote: Priority and **posteriority** in our ideas of time depend upon the constant succession of fleeting perceptions in the mind.

posterity.md.primary: All future generations of people regarded collectively; or all descendants springing from a common ancestor.
posterity.md.secondary: In political philosophy and monumental literature, the aggregate judgment of historical successor generations upon civic deeds.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: To say within thine own deep-sunken eyes, were an all-eating shame and thriftless praise. How much more praise deserv'd thy beauty's use, if thou couldst answer 'This fair child of mine shall sum my count and make my old excuse,' proving his beauty by succession thine! This were to be new made when thou art old, and see thy blood warm when thou feel'st it cold. So thou, through windows of thine age, shall see, despite of wrinkles, this thy golden time: But if thou live, remember'd not to be, die single, and thine image dies with thee, leaving no child to tell **posterity**.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: He lived with an eye toward **posterity**, trusting that future ages would appreciate the scholarly labours ignored by his contemporaries.

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: Whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist; he must plant his convictions firmly, leaving his reputation to impartial **posterity**.

postern.md.primary: A private, secondary back door or rear gate, especially one located inconspicuously in a castle, fort, or city wall.
postern.md.secondary: In medieval military architecture, a concealed sally-port or subterranean defensive wicket permitting secret ingress and egress during sieges.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Good my lord, be piloted by me, and start your flight through the garden **postern** ere the guards be roused.

quotes.author: Walter Scott
quotes.quote: The black knight led his followers through the secluded **postern** gate under the cover of dense midnight mist.

quotes.author: Mrs. Oliphant
quotes.quote: She slipped quietly out through the garden **postern**, eager to escape the inquisitive glances of the village callers.

postexilic.md.primary: Belonging, relating, or subsequent to the period in Jewish history following the Babylonian Exile (after circa 538 BCE).
postexilic.md.secondary: In biblical hermeneutics and ancient Near Eastern historiography, denoting prophetic literature, temple reconstruction, and liturgical reforms after the return to Judah.

quotes.author: James Joyce
quotes.quote: He contemplated the solemn dispersal of Israel and the rebuilding of the second sanctuary during the **postexilic** reconstruction.

quotes.author: Ernest Renan
quotes.work: History of the People of Israel
quotes.quote: The profound transformation of Hebrew religious consciousness was forged during the **postexilic** assemblies guided by Ezra.

quotes.author: Matthew Arnold
quotes.quote: The later Psalms reflect the poignant ethical and spiritual yearnings characteristic of **postexilic** Judaism.

postgraduate.md.primary: Relating to academic study or research undertaken after receiving a bachelor's degree or first university graduation.
postgraduate.md.secondary: In higher education administration, denoting advanced candidates pursuing master's or doctoral theses, or professional post-licensure fellowships.

quotes.author: William James
quotes.quote: Our university laboratories attract brilliant **postgraduate** students dedicated to rigorous experimental investigation of mental phenomena.

quotes.author: H. G. Wells
quotes.quote: He immersed himself in **postgraduate** research at London, investigating economic histories with tireless intellectual ambition.

quotes.author: George Bernard Shaw
quotes.quote: Young physicians attended advanced **postgraduate** clinics to master the newest bacteriological techniques emerging from the continent.

posthumous.md.primary: Occurring, published, awarded, or born after the death of the originator, author, or father.
posthumous.md.secondary: In literary publishing and jurisprudence, designating manuscripts printed following a writer's decease, or legal entitlements vested in a child born after paternal demise.

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: The neglected poet lived in obscurity, leaving his masterpieces to reap a dazzling **posthumous** fame.

quotes.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
quotes.quote: He rummaged through the dusty escritoire, examining the manuscripts reserved for **posthumous** publication.

quotes.author: Washington Irving
quotes.quote: The antiquary devoted his retirement to collecting the scattered papers of the deceased scholar for a **posthumous** volume.

posthumously.md.primary: In a manner occurring, published, awarded, or recognized following a person's death.
posthumously.md.secondary: In biographical history and literary heritage, the conferral of honors, military decorations, or academic editions after the honoree's demise.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: The reclusive verses were printed **posthumously** by loyal friends who recognized the uncelebrated genius of the rural schoolmaster.

quotes.author: Virginia Woolf
quotes.quote: Her intimate diaries were published **posthumously**, revealing a vibrant internal brilliance unsuspected by casual acquaintances.

quotes.author: H. G. Wells
quotes.quote: The philosophical reflections of his brother were edited and issued **posthumously** to critical acclaim.

postiche.md.primary: An artificial piece of hair, toupee, wig, or decorative hairpiece used for theatrical disguise, cosmetic adornment, or vanity.
postiche.md.secondary: In decorative arts and sculpture, an inappropriate, counterfeit, or artificial addition affixed to an authentic antique composition.

quotes.author: Oscar Wilde
quotes.quote: He studied the theatrical actor adjust his powdered wig and ornate **postiche** before the illuminated dressing-room mirror.

quotes.author: Edith Wharton
quotes.quote: The dowager arranged her elaborate curls, concealing sparse silver strands beneath a discreet French **postiche**.

quotes.author: Walter Pater
quotes.quote: The discerning critic observed that the newly added marble drapery was a tasteless **postiche** alien to classical Roman simplicity.

postictal.md.primary: Relating to or occurring in the altered state of consciousness and recovery period immediately following an epileptic seizure.
postictal.md.secondary: In clinical neurology and emergency medicine, characterizing the transient phase of lethargy, confusion, headache, or focal neurological deficit (Todd's paresis) after convulsions.

quotes.author: William Osler
quotes.work: The Principles and Practice of Medicine
quotes.quote: During the **postictal** stupor that succeeds a severe grand mal convulsion, the patient lies flaccid with stertorous respiration.

quotes.author: Arthur Guyton
quotes.quote: The profound cerebral exhaustion observed in the **postictal** state reflects temporary depletion of intracellular energy stores and neurotransmitter exhaustion.

quotes.author: Harvey Cushing
quotes.work: The Pituitary Body and Its Disorders
quotes.quote: Careful neurological examination during the **postictal** interval revealed transient contralateral hemiparesis localized to the cortical lesion.

postilion.md.primary: A rider mounted on the left-hand or near horse of a pair drawing a carriage, coach, or post-chaise to guide the team.
postilion.md.secondary: In transport history, an agile equestrian courier employed instead of a box-seat coachman on long-distance relay mail coaches and aristocratic carriages.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: The **postilion** cracked his whip merrily as the fresh horses sprang forward along the smooth turnpike road.

quotes.author: Charles Dickens
quotes.quote: The mounted **postilion** urged the steaming beasts up the steep incline of the Dover road through the November gloom.

quotes.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotes.quote: Becky Sharp leaned from the chaise window, bidding the jaunty French **postilion** gallop swiftly toward the frontier.

postillion.md.primary: A variant spelling of postilion; a person who rides one of the leading horses pulling a carriage to direct the team.
postillion.md.secondary: In eighteenth-century postal history and travel literature, a guide riding the near leader of a carriage team on post-horse highways.

quotes.author: Tobias Smollett
quotes.quote: Our reckless **postillion** drove with such furious speed over the stony highway that the carriage springs nearly snapped asunder.

quotes.author: Thomas V. Cooper
quotes.quote: The swift dispatches of the Continental Congress were hurried forward by trusty mounted couriers and **postillion** relays.

quotes.author: Walter Scott
quotes.quote: Jeanie Deans watched the breathless **postillion** dismount at the posting inn to change horses under the flickering lantern light.

postimpressionist.md.primary: An artist associated with the late nineteenth-century movement that developed out of Impressionism, emphasizing symbolic content, formal structure, and expressive color.
postimpressionist.md.secondary: In modern art history and aesthetic theory, designating masters such as Cézanne, Gauguin, and Van Gogh who rejected optical naturalism in favor of emotional geometry and psychological resonance.

quotes.author: Roger Fry
quotes.quote: The visionary **postimpressionist** painters rejected mere optical illusion to reveal the underlying architecture of visual emotion.

quotes.author: Clive Bell
quotes.quote: Cézanne stands as the supreme **postimpressionist** master whose canvases awaken direct aesthetic apprehension through significant form.

quotes.author: Virginia Woolf
quotes.quote: The London galleries were convulsed when the radical works of each French **postimpressionist** were first hung before the bewildered public.

postindustrial.md.primary: Relating to or denoting an economy or society in which service, technological, and informational sectors have superseded heavy manufacturing.
postindustrial.md.secondary: In sociological theory and political economy, an advanced developmental stage characterized by knowledge production, digital automation, white-collar labor, and decentralized capital.

quotes.author: Daniel Bell
quotes.quote: In the emerging **postindustrial** order, intellectual technology and technical competence displace property and machinery as the primary sources of structural power.

quotes.author: John Kenneth Galbraith
quotes.quote: The transition toward a **postindustrial** landscape alters the bargaining leverage of organized industrial trade unions.

quotes.author: Alvin Toffler
quotes.quote: Knowledge workers in a **postindustrial** community must adapt continuously to unprecedented accelerations of technological change.

posting.md.primary: The act of traveling rapidly with post horses; displaying a notice in a public place; or entering an item in a ledger.
posting.md.secondary: In bookkeeping and accounting, the formal transference of transactional debit and credit entries from daily journals to permanent accounts in the general ledger.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: From the dull bearer of my love away, my horse with speed doth pace. Then can no horse with my desire keep pace; therefore desire of love's **posting** needs no spur.

quotes.author: Bram Stoker
quotes.quote: We arranged for swift **posting** carriages to bear us across the desolate mountain passes toward the river gorge.

quotes.author: Thomas Henry Huxley
quotes.quote: Scientific method requires meticulous **posting** of empirical observations into classified records without partisan bias.

postlude.md.primary: A concluding musical piece played at the end of a church service, liturgical ceremony, or musical composition.
postlude.md.secondary: In musical composition and literary criticism, a reflective instrumental coda or epilogue that provides formal closure to an extended dramatic work.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: The parish organist concluded the solemn vesper service with a triumphant, resounding **postlude** that filled the vaulted stone arches.

quotes.author: George Bernard Shaw
quotes.quote: The quiet organ **postlude** provided a thoughtful meditation following the exuberant choruses of Handel's oratorio.

quotes.author: E. M. Forster
quotes.quote: The final movement died away into silence, leaving in the air the lingering serenity of an exquisite symphonic **postlude**.

postman.md.primary: A male mail carrier employed by the postal authority to collect, sort, and deliver letters and parcels to residential and business addresses.
postman.md.secondary: In British legal history, one of the two senior junior barristers in the Court of Exchequer holding traditional precedence of motion.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: The village **postman** trudged along the muddy lane, carrying the daily mailbag upon his shoulder through the drizzling mist.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: The arrival of the rural **postman** at the green gate always brought an eager crowd of cottagers awaiting tidings from distant towns.

quotes.author: Herman Melville
quotes.quote: The prompt Wall Street **postman** hurried through the shadowy corridor, tossing packets of correspondence upon our office table.

postmark.md.primary: An official postal cancellation mark stamped upon a letter or parcel indicating the origin, date, and time of mailing.
postmark.md.secondary: In philately and legal evidentiary rules, an indelible postal imprint establishing prima facie verification of the exact time and place an instrument was dispatched.

quotes.author: Jane Austen
quotes.quote: Elinor examined the London **postmark** with an anxious eye, eager to verify when the long-delayed dispatch had been deposited.

quotes.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotes.quote: The envelope bore a blurred provincial **postmark**, but the sharp eye of Holmes instantly identified the date of posting.

quotes.author: G. K. Chesterton
quotes.quote: Father Brown held the mysterious envelope to the lamp, deciphering the faint purple **postmark** stamped across the foreign stamp.

postmaster.md.primary: The official in charge of a local post office, responsible for overseeing the processing, dispatch, and delivery of mail.
postmaster.md.secondary: Historically, an innkeeper or officer licensed to supply post horses, chaises, and riders for travelers along royal dispatch routes.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: I have dogg'd him like his murderer. He does obey every point of the letter that I dropp'd to betray him. He will come to the **postmaster** for fresh mounts.

quotes.author: Charles Dickens
quotes.quote: The bustling village **postmaster** sorted the packets behind the brass grille, regaling his neighbors with scraps of official news.

quotes.author: graf Leo Tolstoy
quotes.quote: Pierre inquired of the station **postmaster** whether fresh horses could be harnessed to continue his journey through the night.

postmenopausal.md.primary: Occurring, relating to, or characteristic of the phase of life following the permanent cessation of menstruation in human females.
postmenopausal.md.secondary: In reproductive endocrinology and gynecology, designating biological changes, hormonal shifts, and elevated osteoporosis risk associated with diminished ovarian estrogen secretion.

quotes.author: William Osler
quotes.work: The Principles and Practice of Medicine
quotes.quote: In **postmenopausal** women, careful diagnostic attention must be given to systemic bone density and cardiovascular integrity.

quotes.author: Arthur Guyton
quotes.quote: Diminished plasma estrogen concentrations during the **postmenopausal** period stimulate compensatory elevations of pituitary gonadotropins.

quotes.author: Harvey Cushing
quotes.work: The Pituitary Body and Its Disorders
quotes.quote: Symptomatic endocrine disturbances observed in **postmenopausal** subjects frequently mirror localized hypothalamic dysregulation.

postmeridian.md.primary: Occurring in, belonging to, or characteristic of the afternoon; taking place after the sun has crossed the meridian (post meridiem / P.M.).
postmeridian.md.secondary: Figuratively in literary prose, denoting the declining, late, or concluding phase of a human life, era, or historical epoch.

quotes.author: Henry David Thoreau
quotes.work: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers
quotes.quote: The gentle warmth of the **postmeridian** hours bathed the lazy ripples of the river in golden reflections.

quotes.author: Washington Irving
quotes.quote: The squire enjoyed his customary **postmeridian** nap in the high-backed library armchair while the shadows lengthened on the lawn.

quotes.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
quotes.work: The House of the Seven Gables
quotes.quote: In his **postmeridian** years, the old gentleman found tranquility in tending the dusty garden flowers behind the ancestral mansion.

postmillennial.md.primary: Relating to or upholding postmillennialism, the eschatological Christian doctrine that the second coming of Christ occurs after a thousand-year golden era of spiritual prosperity.
postmillennial.md.secondary: In religious historiography and sociological theology, designating optimism regarding the moral and social perfection of human civilization through evangelical reform before the final judgment.

quotes.author: Jonathan Edwards
quotes.work: A History of the Work of Redemption
quotes.quote: The steadfast faith of the church anticipates that **postmillennial** glory wherein the knowledge of God shall cover the whole earth.

quotes.author: John Cairns
quotes.quote: He defended the **postmillennial** hope that gradual Christian education and missionary zeal would banish moral darkness from mankind.

quotes.author: William James
quotes.quote: The exuberant civic optimism of American revivalists was closely linked to their fervent **postmillennial** expectations of earthly righteousness.

postmistress.md.primary: A woman who manages, directs, or holds official appointment over a post office.
postmistress.md.secondary: In social history and rural sociology, an independent female civil servant serving as the confidential communication hub of a provincial community.

quotes.author: James Joyce
quotes.quote: The curious **postmistress** weighed the parcel upon her brass scales, scrutinizing the handwriting with keen provincial interest.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Elfride handed her sealed letter to the elderly village **postmistress**, blushing lest the secret destination be guessed.

quotes.author: Anthony Trollope
quotes.quote: The venerable **postmistress** guarded the royal postbags with fierce administrative pride, brooking no interference from local clergy.

postmodern.md.primary: Relating to or characteristic of a cultural, philosophical, and artistic movement that challenges modernism, meta-narratives, and objective certainties.
postmodern.md.secondary: In critical theory, architecture, and epistemology, emphasizing irony, stylistic pastiche, social constructivism, and skepticism toward foundational claims of universal truth.

quotes.author: Fredric Jameson
quotes.work: Postmodernism, or, the Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism
quotes.quote: The fragmentation of the subject represents a central structural feature of the **postmodern** hyperspace in contemporary culture.

quotes.author: Jean-François Lyotard
quotes.quote: Simplifying to the extreme, I define **postmodern** as incredulity toward grand metanarratives.

quotes.author: Umberto Eco
quotes.work: Postscript to The Name of the Rose
quotes.quote: The **postmodern** reply to the modern consists of recognizing that the past, since it cannot really be destroyed, must be revisited with irony.

postmodernism.md.primary: A late twentieth-century movement in philosophy, arts, and literature characterized by skepticism toward grand narratives, absolute truth, and historical progression.
postmodernism.md.secondary: In cultural sociology and aesthetic theory, an intellectual epoch marked by pluralism, pastiche, intertextuality, hyperreality, and the erosion of boundaries between high and low culture.

quotes.author: David Harvey
quotes.quote: The rise of **postmodernism** signals a fundamental shift in how Western societies experience space, time, and global capital.

quotes.author: Jean Baudrillard
quotes.quote: In the hyperreal realm celebrated by **postmodernism**, the simulation of reality replaces authentic engagement with the world.

quotes.author: Terry Eagleton
quotes.quote: The radical irony championed by **postmodernism** risks disarming genuine political critique by dissolving all normative claims.

postmodernist.md.primary: An adherent, practitioner, or proponent of postmodernism in literature, philosophy, architecture, or the visual arts.
postmodernist.md.secondary: Relating to the stylistic, deconstructive, and relativist methods employed by thinkers and creators who dismantle modernist canons.

quotes.author: Richard Rorty
quotes.quote: The committed **postmodernist** philosopher abandons foundational epistemology to embrace open-ended, pragmatic conversation.

quotes.author: Jürgen Habermas
quotes.quote: The **postmodernist** critique of communicative rationality threatens to undermine the unfinished emancipatory project of the Enlightenment.

quotes.author: Charles Jencks
quotes.quote: The innovative **postmodernist** architect combines classical ornamentation with contemporary irony to create double-coded buildings.

postmortal.md.primary: Occurring, existing, or performed subsequent to physical death; posthumous or postmortem in nature.
postmortal.md.secondary: In eschatological theology and speculative metaphysics, denoting states of spiritual survival, judgment, or continuing consciousness beyond biological demise.

quotes.author: William James
quotes.quote: Human longing has continually posited a **postmortal** existence to redress the moral inequities of earthly experience.

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: The soul disdains temporal limits, looking forward to its sublime **postmortal** destiny across infinite spiritual domains.

quotes.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
quotes.quote: The moral argument for immortality presumes a **postmortal** retribution wherein virtue finds its eternal reward.

postmortem.md.primary: An examination and dissection of a deceased body to determine the cause of death or evaluate pathological changes; an autopsy.
postmortem.md.secondary: In organizational management and project debriefing, a retrospective analytical review conducted following the conclusion of an operation or project to identify failures and successes.

quotes.author: James Joyce
quotes.quote: Good idea a **postmortem** for doctors. See what killed him. Find out the cause of death before burial.

quotes.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotes.quote: The surgeon conducted a thorough **postmortem** examination of the victim, confirming that poison had induced immediate cardiac arrest.

quotes.author: William Osler
quotes.work: The Principles and Practice of Medicine
quotes.quote: Careful correlation between clinical signs and **postmortem** findings remains the bedrock of rigorous pathology.

postnatal.md.primary: Occurring, relating to, or administered during the period immediately following childbirth, especially concerning infant development or maternal recovery.
postnatal.md.secondary: In developmental pediatrics and obstetrical medicine, denoting physiological adaptations, metabolic screening, and neurological maturation during the initial weeks of neonatal life.

quotes.author: William Osler
quotes.work: The Principles and Practice of Medicine
quotes.quote: Careful supervision during the **postnatal** convalescence prevents septic complications in both mother and newborn.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.quote: The extended period of **postnatal** helplessness in human infants necessitates prolonged parental care and mutual social cooperation.

quotes.author: Arthur Guyton
quotes.quote: Immediate circulatory adjustments during the early **postnatal** minutes include functional closure of the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale.

postnuptial.md.primary: Made, occurring, or executed following the solemnization of a marriage, especially regarding agreements governing marital property.
postnuptial.md.secondary: In family law and estate jurisprudence, a formal contract executed between spouses establishing property division and financial support in the event of divorce or death.

quotes.author: William Blackstone
quotes.work: Commentaries on the Laws of England
quotes.quote: A voluntary **postnuptial** settlement executed by a husband upon his wife will be sustained in equity if free from fraud against creditors.

quotes.author: Anthony Trollope
quotes.quote: The family solicitors drafted a comprehensive **postnuptial** covenant to safeguard the lady's independent fortune.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Questions arose among the trustees concerning the legal validity of the disputed **postnuptial** agreement.

postoperative.md.primary: Relating to, occurring during, or administered throughout the period following a surgical operation.
postoperative.md.secondary: In surgical critical care, protocols directed toward wound healing, pain management, hemodynamics, and prevention of thromboembolic or pulmonary complications.

quotes.author: Harvey Cushing
quotes.work: The Pituitary Body and Its Disorders
quotes.quote: Vigilant management during the immediate **postoperative** period ensured rapid restoration of cerebral functions without intracranial hemorrhage.

quotes.author: William Osler
quotes.work: The Principles and Practice of Medicine
quotes.quote: The introduction of strict antiseptic technique drastically reduced the incidence of severe **postoperative** sepsis in hospital wards.

quotes.author: Arthur Guyton
quotes.quote: Systemic fluid balance requires careful monitoring during the early **postoperative** hours to counteract transient surgical shock.

postoperatively.md.primary: In a manner occurring, performed, or administered during the convalescent period following surgical intervention.
postoperatively.md.secondary: In surgical nursing and clinical pharmacology, referring to the timeline and execution of therapies, analgesic titrations, and rehabilitative ambulation subsequent to surgery.

quotes.author: Harvey Cushing
quotes.quote: The patient was managed **postoperatively** with mild sedation and elevation of the head of the bed to facilitate venous drainage.

quotes.author: William Osler
quotes.work: The Principles and Practice of Medicine
quotes.quote: When treated **postoperatively** with appropriate supportive therapy, surgical mortality declined significantly across clinical services.

quotes.author: Alexander Fleming
quotes.quote: Administering antibiotics **postoperatively** halted secondary bacteremia in high-risk abdominal procedures.

postpone.md.primary: To defer, delay, or put off an event, action, or appointment to a later date or future time.
postpone.md.secondary: In organizational planning and legislative procedure, to table a motion or suspend deliberations until predetermined conditions or inquiries are met.

quotes.author: John Stuart Mill
quotes.quote: We may **postpone** the final judgment upon controversial opinions until complete evidence can be gathered and examined.

quotes.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotes.quote: We must not **postpone** our arrival in Devonshire by a single unnecessary hour, lest grave peril befall our companion.

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: Do not **postpone** the heroic resolution of the present hour in the deceptive hope of a more convenient morrow.

postponement.md.primary: The act of putting off, deferring, or delaying an event, scheduled meeting, or planned action to a future time.
postponement.md.secondary: In judicial procedure and treaty negotiation, a formal stay of proceedings or continuance granted by a tribunal to allow adequate preparation.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Every day brought fresh reasons for the **postponement** of their departure from the sequestered valley.

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: The soul resists that fatal **postponement** of duty which wastes life in anticipation of ideal circumstances.

quotes.author: Bram Stoker
quotes.quote: The brief **postponement** of our expedition gave Jonathan time to recover his shattered physical strength.

postponer.md.primary: A person who habitually puts off, defers, or procrastinates performing obligations, tasks, or necessary decisions.
postponer.md.secondary: In moral psychology and behavioral ethics, an individual who avoids present discomfort or responsibility through chronic postponement and evasion.

quotes.author: Samuel Johnson
quotes.quote: The habitual **postponer** of virtuous exertion flatters himself that tomorrow will bring clarity, while habit cements his indolence.

quotes.author: William James
quotes.quote: The chronic **postponer** suffers an exhausting paralysis of volition, endlessly deliberating while opportunity slips away.

quotes.author: Charles Dickens
quotes.quote: Mr. Micawber, that eternal **postponer** of practical decisions, sat waiting serenely for something profitable to turn up.

postscript.md.primary: An additional sentence, paragraph, or message appended to a letter after the writer's signature (commonly abbreviated P.S.).
postscript.md.secondary: In literary criticism and scholarly editions, a supplementary note, epilogue, or afterword appended to a treatise or book to address subsequent developments.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: Jove knows I love, but who? Lips do not move, no man must know. What follows? The numbers altered! No man must know! If this should be thee, Malvolio! Soft, here follows prose: If this fall into thy hand, revolve. In my stars I am above thee, but be not afraid of greatness. Read the **postscript**.

quotes.author: Charles Dickens
quotes.quote: Our guardian added a brief, affectionate **postscript** to his letter, reassuring us that all was well at the country estate.

quotes.author: Jane Austen
quotes.quote: Elizabeth read the hasty **postscript** with intense relief, learning that her sister had safely reached town.

postulant.md.primary: A candidate or applicant seeking admission into a religious order or monastic community, undergoing an initial period of discernment.
postulant.md.secondary: In canon law and ecclesiastic administration, a probationary novice who lives within a monastic convent prior to taking canonical vows.

quotes.author: graf Leo Tolstoy
quotes.quote: The humble **postulant** bowed reverently before the elder, seeking spiritual guidance in the quiet monastic cell.

quotes.author: James Joyce
quotes.work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
quotes.quote: He imagined the solemn quiet of the cloister, where a devout **postulant** dedicated every waking hour to meditation and prayer.

quotes.author: Charlotte Brontë
quotes.quote: The convent gates opened to receive the youthful **postulant**, whose pale face reflected sincere spiritual resolution.

postulate.md.primary: To claim, demand, or assume the truth or existence of something as a necessary basis for reasoning, discussion, or belief.
postulate.md.secondary: In formal logic, geometry, and axiomatic philosophy, a fundamental proposition or axiom taken as self-evident without proof to ground a deductively valid system.

quotes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
quotes.quote: We **postulate** a spiritual unity in the universe that harmonizes the apparent contradictions of material phenomena.

quotes.author: James George Frazer
quotes.quote: Primitive magicians **postulate** an invisible sympathetic connection between physical objects that have once been in contact.

quotes.author: John Stuart Mill
quotes.quote: Geometric demonstrations must necessarily **postulate** certain primary definitions and spatial relations as starting points.

postulation.md.primary: The act of asserting, proposing, or assuming a principle or hypothesis as the starting point for logical reasoning or inquiry.
postulation.md.secondary: In theoretical physics, epistemology, and ecclesiastical law, an axiomatic assertion grounding an explanatory model; or a formal petition for canonical appointment.

quotes.author: Francis Bacon
quotes.quote: True natural philosophy rejects arbitrary **postulation**, requiring empirical induction grounded in systematic experimentation.

quotes.author: John Locke
quotes.quote: The dogmatic **postulation** of innate ideas hinders the open advancement of genuine scientific inquiry.

quotes.author: William James
quotes.quote: The fundamental **postulation** of cognitive psychology assumes that mental states correspond directly to neural events.

postulational.md.primary: Of, relating to, or derived from postulates or foundational axiomatic assumptions.
postulational.md.secondary: In formal mathematics, logic, and philosophy of science, characterizing methods that construct deductive theoretical frameworks from a defined set of primitive axioms.

quotes.author: Bertrand Russell
quotes.quote: The **postulational** method offers great advantages of logical elegance, though it cannot manufacture empirical truth out of thin air.

quotes.author: Alfred North Whitehead
quotes.quote: Every systematic cosmology must establish its **postulational** foundations before deducing the intricate relations of actual entities.

quotes.author: Charles Sanders Peirce
quotes.quote: Rigorous scientific hypothesis differs from dogmatic assertion by treating its **postulational** principles as subject to empirical verification.

postulator.md.primary: A person who proposes, advocates, or postulates a principle, hypothesis, or petition.
postulator.md.secondary: In Roman Catholic canon law, an official advocate appointed to petition the Holy See and assemble historical and theological evidence for the beatification and canonization of a servant of God.

quotes.author: Edward Gibbon
quotes.work: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
quotes.quote: The ecclesiastical **postulator** pleaded before the papal congregation, reciting the miracles attributed to the venerated martyr.

quotes.author: John Henry Newman
quotes.quote: The canonical **postulator** marshaled documentary evidence to establish the heroic virtues of the revered founder.

quotes.author: Lord Acton
quotes.quote: In Roman causes, the **postulator** must examine every contradictory testimony to withstand the objections of the promotor fidei.

postum.md.primary: A popular roasted-grain caffeine-free beverage brand developed by C. W. Post in 1895 as a healthy coffee alternative.
postum.md.secondary: In commercial dietary history and industrial food manufacture, an instant hot drink powder prepared from roasted wheat bran, wheat berries, and molasses.

quotes.author: Thorstein Veblen
quotes.work: The Theory of the Leisure Class
quotes.quote: Modern advertising transformed wholesome grain substitutes such as **Postum** into household staples of temperance culture.

quotes.author: Sinclair Lewis
quotes.quote: He drank his steaming cup of cereal **Postum** with virtuous satisfaction, commending its digestive mildness to his household.

quotes.author: John Dos Passos
quotes.quote: Billboards along the midwestern railroad tracks proclaimed the hygienic virtues of **Postum** to weary morning commuters.

postural.md.primary: Relating to, involving, or affecting physical posture and the alignment or bearing of the body.
postural.md.secondary: In neurophysiology and kinesiology, denoting automatic neuromuscular reflexes, vestibular mechanisms, and muscle tone maintaining balance against gravitational force.

quotes.author: William Osler
quotes.work: The Principles and Practice of Medicine
quotes.quote: Faulty **postural** habits among sedentary youths frequently contribute to progressive spinal deformities and chest restriction.

quotes.author: Arthur Guyton
quotes.quote: The brainstem reticular nuclei coordinate continuous **postural** reflexes to preserve upright equilibrium during locomotion.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.work: The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals
quotes.quote: Instinctive **postural** adjustments in threatened animals serve either to intimidate predators or signal submissive retreat.

posture.md.primary: The position, carriage, or disposition in which the body is held, whether sitting, standing, or moving.
posture.md.secondary: A deliberate mental attitude, moral stance, or strategic diplomatic disposition adopted to convey intent or project capability.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: The **posture** of your blows are yet unknown; but for your words, they rob the Hybla bees, and leave them honeyless.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Clym preserved his meditative **posture** beside the hearth, gazing deeply into the red embers of the turf fire.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: The weaver sat crouched over his loom in a rigid **posture** that had become second nature through thirty years of solitary toil.

posturer.md.primary: A person who affects artificial poses, insincere attitudes, or theatrical mannerisms to impress or mislead others.
posturer.md.secondary: In social satire and dramatic theory, an exhibitionist or charlatan whose public demeanor consists of affected poses lacking genuine depth.

quotes.author: William Makepeace Thackeray
quotes.quote: Society is crowded with vain **posturers** who mimic the manners of peers while despising their own honest origins.

quotes.author: George Bernard Shaw
quotes.quote: The fashionable romantic actor proved himself a hollow **posturer**, striking melodramatic poses in place of tragic passion.

quotes.author: Thomas Carlyle
quotes.quote: A sincere hero commands reverence, but the shallow **posturer** excites only momentary amusement followed by contempt.

posturing.md.primary: Behavior that is affected, theatrical, or intended to create a misleading impression of importance, courage, or piety.
posturing.md.secondary: In political communication and social psychology, the strategic display of exaggerated rhetoric, stances, or moral poses to influence public perception.

quotes.author: Charles Dickens
quotes.quote: Mr. Pumblechook engaged in absurd **posturing** before the company, claiming the entire credit for Pip's sudden good fortune.

quotes.author: Meyer Moldeven
quotes.quote: Beneath all the political **posturing** and fiery rhetoric, the fundamental economic realities remained completely unchanged.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.quote: Lydgate despised the petty **posturing** of provincial practitioners who courted popularity through pompous medical jargon.

preposterous.md.primary: Contrary to reason, common sense, or nature; absurd, ridiculous, or bizarre in the highest degree.
preposterous.md.secondary: Etymologically, having that first which ought to be last; completely inverted in natural order, sequence, or moral priority.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: **Preposterous** ass, that never read so far to know the cause why music was ordain'd! Was it not to refresh the mind of man after his studies and his usual pain?

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.quote: Boldwood dismissed the bizarre rumor as a **preposterous** fabrication unworthy of a single moment's serious thought.

quotes.author: Charles Darwin
quotes.quote: It seems at first **preposterous** to suppose that so complex an organ as the eye could have been formed by natural selection.

preposterously.md.primary: In an absurd, foolish, irrational, or highly ridiculous manner.
preposterously.md.secondary: In rhetoric and social critique, acting with comical perversity or inverted judgment so egregious as to excite derision.

quotes.author: William Shakespeare
quotes.quote: And those things do best please me that befall **preposterously**.

quotes.author: Robert Browning
quotes.quote: The witness contradicted himself **preposterously**, shifting his story with every cross-examination from the magistrate.

quotes.author: Charles Dickens
quotes.quote: Mr. Winkle dressed himself **preposterously** in sporting attire that aroused the sarcastic merriment of the village youths.
